title: My God, my God (Psalm 22)
hook: a cry of abandonment that turns to praise; Jesus prayed its first line on the cross

segments.voice: Yesterday, the firmament declaring God's glory without a word. Your line was day unto day, speech. What did the sky say to you? Day four hundred sixteen.

Some days the psalms are sunrises and pleasant places. Today's isn't. Today's begins in the dark, with a sentence people have said, or wanted to say, at a graveside, in an empty kitchen, in the small hours when prayers seem to hit the ceiling and fall back down. It's the opening of Psalm twenty-two. And the reason it's so famous is not only what it says. It's who said it, long after it was written, hanging on a Roman cross outside Jerusalem, near the end.
screen: `TODAY BEGINS IN THE DARK.` → `PRAYERS THAT HIT THE CEILING.` → `WHO SAID IT, ON A CROSS.`

segments.voice: The psalm begins, in the King James Bible: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?" Roaring. Not a polite complaint. A howl. And notice it still says my God, twice. Even the cry of abandonment is addressed to God. The psalmist doesn't walk away. He shouts toward the One who seems absent. Then the psalm gets very physical. Surrounded by enemies like bulls and dogs. Bones out of joint. A tongue stuck to the jaw. "They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture." The Gospels tell the crucifixion with this psalm close by: the mocking crowd, the thirst, and the soldiers gambling for Jesus' clothes, which John's Gospel says fulfilled this very line. And Matthew and Mark both record that near the end, Jesus cried out the first line: "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Christians read that cry in more than one way. Some hear real anguish: Jesus entering the deepest human darkness, the feeling of being forsaken, so that no one is ever alone in it again. Others point out that quoting the first line of a psalm could call the whole psalm to mind. And the whole psalm doesn't end in the dark. Around verse twenty-two it turns: "I will declare thy name unto my brethren: in the midst of the congregation will I praise thee." The cry becomes a song, and by the end, the psalm reaches the ends of the earth and generations not yet born. Plenty of Christians hold both readings at once. The cry is real. And the psalm itself doesn't stop at the cry.
screen: `MY GOD, TWICE, EVEN IN THE DARK.` · `GARMENTS PARTED, LOTS CAST.` · `ELI, ELI, LAMA SABACHTHANI.` · `THE CRY TURNS TO PRAISE.` · then, large: `MY GOD, MY GOD, WHY HAST THOU FORSAKEN ME?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the first line honestly. Settle, and breathe. If there's something in your life right now that feels like abandonment, a loss, a silence, an unanswered prayer, let it come up. You don't have to tidy it. If you pray, you can say the first line, slowly, and mean it: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? Notice you're still saying my God. If you don't pray, simply name the hard thing honestly, out loud or inside, without pretending it's fine. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
My God. The first words of Psalm twenty-two, a cry of abandonment that still calls God mine, and that Jesus prayed on the cross.
Your line: even he cried this. Today, if someone tells you they feel forsaken, don't hurry them out of it. Sit with them in the first line. Day four hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Some churches read Psalm 22 on Good Friday, and in some traditions the altar is stripped on Maundy Thursday while it is said or sung; Christians also pray its first line in times of grief.

fork.setup: you feel completely abandoned by God. the psalmist felt the same. what does he do?
options: cry out to God, calling him my God.
fork.reveal: he howls at God and still says my God, twice. and later in the same psalm, the cry turns to praise.

original.note: Hebrew of Psalm 22:1. On the cross, the Gospels give it in Aramaic: lama sabachthani.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus lost faith on the cross.
what it means: he prayed the opening of a psalm that cries out to 'my God' and ends in praise.
what a scholar hears: Hebrew azavtani, Aramaic sabachthani; quoting a psalm's first line could call the whole psalm to mind.
recall: a food their fathers never knew

notes: Editor review (y2 days 407–424): hook drops "many people", the uncited "centuries after it was written", and the hospital image repeated on days 418 and 423; the garments line now rests on John 19:24, which quotes it; "in Aramaic" removed from the teach (Matthew's Eli is closer to Hebrew); "many hear / many also notice" changed to some/others; narrator's verdict "Both readings hold" and stock "isn't the last word" replaced; practice renamed so it isn't an instruction to pray; howItsDone and myth softened.
The date of Psalm 22 is uncertain (traditionally David, c. 1000 BC); the script says 'centuries after it was written'.
Matthew 27:46 has 'Eli, Eli'; Mark 15:34 'Eloi, Eloi'. The Gospel forms mix Hebrew and Aramaic; the script says 'in Aramaic'. Confirm.
The two readings of the cry (real anguish; citing the whole psalm) given without ranking. Confirm.
Psalm 22:16 'they pierced my hands and my feet' is deliberately not quoted because the Hebrew text is disputed (ka'ari, 'like a lion'); a Keeper may want to address it.
Maundy Thursday stripping of the altar with Psalm 22: practice in Anglican, Lutheran and some Catholic settings; confirm howItsDone wording.
